h1: How long an opened bottle of wine lasts and how to keep it fresh
title: How Long Opened Wine Lasts | Craft Beer School
desc: How long an opened bottle of red, white, sparkling or fortified wine stays good, why it fades and simple ways to keep it fresh.
teaser: Most opened wine is fine for a few days if you recork it and put it in the fridge. Even the red.
standfirst: Opened a bottle and not finished it? Wine starts to change the moment air reaches it, but you have more time than you might think. Here is how long each style lasts and how to stretch it.
sections:
Two things happen to wine once the bottle is open.

  • Oxidation. Oxygen reacts with the wine. Fresh fruit aromas fade, the wine tastes flat and whites slowly turn deeper yellow. With time a nutty, bruised apple note appears, from a compound called acetaldehyde.
  • Acetic spoilage. Acetic acid bacteria, carried by air and fruit flies, turn alcohol into acetic acid. Leave a half-full bottle open long enough on a warm counter and it heads towards vinegar.

Both processes speed up with heat. That makes the Indian kitchen counter the worst place to keep an opened bottle. Beer drinkers will recognise the same chemistry from our guide to oxidised beer.

These are typical times for a bottle recorked and kept in the fridge.

  • Sparkling wine. 1 to 3 days with a proper sparkling stopper. Bubbles fade first.
  • Light whites and rosé. 3 to 5 days.
  • Full-bodied whites. 3 to 5 days. Oaked whites sometimes hold slightly better.
  • Red wines. 3 to 5 days. Tannic reds often hold longer than light ones. Some even taste better on day two.
  • Sweet wines. Up to a week or so, as sugar and often higher sulphur dioxide help protect them.
  • Fortified wines. Light fino and manzanilla sherry only a few days, like white wine. Tawny port and oxidative styles keep for weeks, because they were deliberately aged with oxygen already.
  • Bag-in-box wine. Several weeks, because the bag collapses as wine is poured and air does not get in.
The fridge is the best tool you have

Most people keep reds on the counter because that is what they were told. In a cool European kitchen that works. In an Indian one it does not. The single most effective step is to put the bottle in the fridge, red wine included. Cold slows both oxidation and bacteria sharply. A red kept on the counter in a Delhi summer can taste tired by the next evening. The same wine recorked and refrigerated is usually still good three days later.

Take a red out of the fridge about 20 to 30 minutes before you drink it, so it can warm to around 14 to 18 °C. Our guide to wine storage in India covers unopened bottles too.
Simple ways to keep it fresh longer

• Plan ahead. If you only want a glass or two, pour what you need and put the rest away at once, rather than after the meal.
  • Recork straight away. Do not leave the bottle open on the table through a long dinner if you know you will not finish it.
  • Reduce the air space. Pour leftovers into a smaller clean bottle with a screw cap, filled close to the top. Less air means slower oxidation.
  • Vacuum stoppers. Hand pumps remove some air. They help a little but do not create a true vacuum, so results are modest.
  • Inert gas. Argon sprays and preservation systems displace air from the bottle. They work better than vacuum pumps and are popular in bars that pour by the glass.
  • Proper sparkling stoppers. A spoon in the neck does nothing. A clamp-style stopper holds pressure.
How to tell if it has gone

Smell it before you pour a glass. Your nose picks up these changes long before your tongue does.

  • Flat, muted fruit with a dull colour: oxidised, but harmless. Use it for cooking.
  • Bruised apple, sherry-like notes in a wine that should be fresh: well oxidised.
  • Sharp vinegar or nail varnish smell: acetic spoilage. Pour it away.

Our guide to wine faults covers these and other problems in more detail. Slightly tired wine is still fine in a pasta sauce, a mushroom dish or a slow-cooked Goan pork curry, where the cooking hides the faded fruit.
Why some wines last longer than others

The differences between styles are not random. Acidity, tannin, sugar, alcohol and sulphur dioxide all protect wine against oxygen. A winemaker chooses these levels deliberately. That choice decides how a wine holds up after opening.

Understanding those choices also explains why some wines age for decades in the bottle while others are meant to be drunk within a year. That story starts in the cellar, long before the cork comes out.
faqs: Should opened red wine go in the fridge?
Yes. Cold slows oxidation and bacteria. Take it out 20 to 30 minutes before drinking so it is not served too cold.
Can I drink wine that was opened a week ago?
It is unlikely to harm you but will probably taste flat or sour. If it smells of vinegar, pour it away. Otherwise it may still be fine for cooking.
